title: Ektaa Kapoor Recalls Being Mocked for Tilak, Calls Out Bollywood 'Hinduphobia'
excerpt: On Ranveer Allahbadia's podcast, the producer said she was labelled a freak for wearing a tika and sacred threads, and argued that Hindu folklore faces scrutiny Western fantasy does not.
body:
• Producer Ektaa Kapoor has described what she calls deep-rooted "Hinduphobia" in Bollywood, in a podcast conversation with Ranveer Allahbadia.
  • She recalled being judged and labelled a freak when younger for wearing a tika and sacred threads, and for visiting a temple before going to a club.
  • Her comments are tied to her folklore film The Vvaan: Force Of The Forrest, released in theatres on September 25.
  • Kapoor says acceptance of Indian folklore and mythology on screen is now growing, after years in which she felt such stories faced extra scrutiny.

Producer Ektaa Kapoor has called out what she describes as "Hinduphobia" in Bollywood, questioning why stories rooted in Hindu mythology and folklore face scrutiny that Western-inspired fantasy does not. Speaking on a podcast with Ranveer Allahbadia, she also recalled being mocked earlier in her career for wearing a tika and sacred threads, according to India Forums.

Kapoor argued that the industry is comfortable with animation and imported fantasy concepts while treating Indian folklore as a problem to be explained. She said the numbers for her film The Vvaan were strong, but that what mattered more to her was that the film deals with folklore at all, and she pointed to what she sees as growing acceptance of such narratives, as reported by The Film Window.

Mocked for Wearing Her Faith Openly

Kapoor, who is well known for wearing several rings, bracelets and sacred threads, said openly displaying her faith was not always received positively when she was younger. Wearing a tika, she recalled, could be enough for people around her to label someone a freak, and she described the discomfort she encountered when her religious practice met her professional and social life.

"Wearing a tika and wearing your religion on your sleeve is such a problem."

— Ektaa Kapoor, Producer

She recounted one incident in which people reacted with surprise on learning she had visited a temple before heading to a club, as if devotion and a modern social life could not coexist. Her response, then and now, was to ask what exactly was shocking about it. The anecdote, she suggested, captures the assumption she has spent years pushing against: that visible Hindu practice is somehow at odds with a contemporary entertainment career.

Rooted Stories and The Vvaan

The remarks are closely tied to The Vvaan: Force Of The Forrest, starring Sidharth Malhotra and Tamannaah Bhatia and directed by Deepak Kumar Mishra, with Anup Soni, Sunil Grover, Shweta Tiwari and Maniesh Paul also in the cast. The film blends supernatural elements with Indian folklore, drawing on traditions associated with the Maa Van Devi Temple, and was released in theatres on September 25.

At the film's trailer launch, Kapoor had made a related argument about rooted storytelling, criticising creators she described as out of touch with the common audience and saying the collaboration with Arunabh Kumar of TVF grew out of shared faith — the two, she joked, became "mandir friends," discussing the Bihar-set story about a van devi from one temple to another, Bollywood Hungama reported. Tamannaah Bhatia told the same event that her own priest had praised the film's depiction of Chhath Puja in the song "Chhathi Maiya," and that her watchman had asked about it — the kind of ground-level response Kapoor says rooted stories produce.

Why It Resonates, and What Comes Next

For diaspora audiences, the argument lands in familiar territory. Many Indians abroad negotiate the same visibility Kapoor describes — a tilak at the office Diwali party, a temple visit before a night out — and her claim is that the screen should stop treating that negotiation as an embarrassment. Whether one accepts the word "Hinduphobia" or not, her commercial point is testable: folklore-led films either find audiences or they do not, and she says The Vvaan's numbers support her case.

Kapoor's own assessment is that the environment has shifted, with greater acceptance now allowing filmmakers to explore Indian traditions with more confidence. The next test is slate-level: whether Balaji and other major producers put more folklore and mythology projects into production, rather than treating The Vvaan as a one-off experiment.
